title: A domain tensored with a finite type domain over an algebraically closed field
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, $R$ a commutative $k$-algebra which is a domain, and $S$ a commutative $k$-algebra which is a finite type domain. Then $R\otimes_k S$ is a domain.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 00I7, final paragraph; algebraic coordinate version of its closed-fibre argument

proof.text: Choose a k-basis of R. TensorProduct.basis and its coordinate maps identify each tensor element with a finite family of coordinates in S. Naturality of these coordinates under S-algebra maps follows by tensor induction.

For each maximal ideal m of S, finite_of_finite_type_of_isJacobsonRing makes S/m finite over k. IsAlgClosed.algebraMap_bijective_of_isIntegral identifies S/m with k. Tensor congruence and rid identify R tensor_k (S/m) with R. Thus for xy=0 one specialized tensor element vanishes, so all its coordinates lie in m.

If x and y were nonzero, choose nonzero coordinates a and b. The specialization alternative shows ab belongs to every maximal ideal of S. Since S is Jacobson by isJacobsonRing_of_finiteType [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-field-prime-intersection-maximal], and S is a domain, the Jacobson radical of zero is zero. Hence ab=0 contradicts a,b nonzero.
Algebra.TensorProduct.nontrivial_of_algebraMap_injective_of_isDomain makes the tensor product nontrivial. Combined with the preceding absence of zero divisors, this gives IsDomain.
